Build the Totem Of Undying.

As a Master Teacher, I will guide you through the spatial rationale for constructing the 'Totem Of Undying'. Before we look at a single coordinate, I want you to visualize the physical space and the artistic intent behind this structure. 

Footprint Analysis:
I will build this structure as a vertical, 2D pixel-art sprite. The dimensions are 14 blocks wide along the X-axis, 15 blocks tall along the Y-axis (Y=0 through Y=14), and exactly 1 block deep along the Z-axis. Because it is a 2D representation of an item, it is completely solid, with no hollow interior or 3D tiering. The structure relies entirely on color gradients and outlines to create the illusion of depth and shape.

Material Strategy:
I must carefully select blocks that mimic the metallic and magical properties of the Totem. 
I will use Stripped Acacia Logs for the entire outer border and structural linework. Its warm, orange-brown tone perfectly replicates the bronze/wooden casing of the totem.
For the golden body, I will use a three-part gradient: Gold Blocks for the brightest metallic highlights, Yellow Wool for the mid-tones, and Yellow Terracotta for the darker shadows. This contrast is what gives our flat structure a 3D, rounded appearance.
For the magical eyes, I will use Emerald Blocks for the dark, piercing pupils, surrounded by Lime Wool to simulate a glowing green aura. 
Finally, I will use White Concrete and White Wool to add sharp specular highlights, making the gold and eyes look shiny and reflective.

Construction Sequence & Logic:
I will build this from the ground up, layer by layer, keeping the structure centered.

At Y=0 to Y=2 (The Base): I will start at Y=0 with a narrow 4-block wide base of Stripped Acacia. At Y=1 and Y=2, I will expand the width to 6 blocks, filling the center with Yellow Wool and Terracotta. This forms the bottom peg or 'tail' of the totem.

At Y=3 (The Belt): I will widen the structure to 8 blocks using a solid horizontal line of Stripped Acacia. I am doing this to create a distinct visual separator between the base and the main torso.

At Y=4 to Y=7 (The Torso and Arms): At Y=4, I will build the lower torso using my gold gradient. At Y=5, I will flare the structure out to 12 blocks wide, introducing White Concrete to act as a bright glint on the totem's wrists. At Y=6, I will reach the maximum width of 14 blocks. This layer represents the folded arms or wings of the totem wrapping around its golden belly. At Y=7, I will cap the shoulders with a thick layer of Stripped Acacia, tapering the width back down to 12 blocks.

At Y=8 (The Neck): I will narrow the build back to the core 8-block width. I will use yellow and gold blocks here to form the neck and lower jaw area, preparing for the face.

At Y=9 to Y=10 (The Eyes): This is the focal point of the build. At Y=9, I will place the Emerald Blocks for the pupils, flanked by Lime Wool and White Wool to create the iconic glowing green eyes. At Y=10, I will finish the upper half of the eyes with more Lime and White Wool, keeping everything strictly framed by the Acacia outline.

At Y=11 (The Forehead): I will place a simple layer of Acacia and Yellow Terracotta to act as the forehead, separating the glowing eyes from the crown above.

At Y=12 to Y=14 (The Crown): At Y=12 and Y=13, I will build the golden headpiece. I will cluster Gold Blocks and White Wool on the left side to simulate a strong light source hitting the metal, while transitioning to Yellow Wool on the right side to represent the shadow. Finally, at Y=14, I will cap the entire structure with a 6-block wide line of Stripped Acacia to close the outline and finish the top of the head. 

By following this logic, I ensure that every block serves a purpose, either defining the silhouette or tricking the eye into seeing a shiny, 3D golden artifact.

Build the Desert Home (Small).

As a Master Teacher, I need you to visualize this structure before you ever look at the raw coordinates. We are building the "Desert Home (Small)". This is not a standard wooden box; it is a classic, flat-roofed desert pueblo designed to withstand harsh heat. 

Footprint Analysis:
The overall dimensions of this build are 11 blocks wide (X-axis), 5 blocks deep (Z-axis), and 10 blocks tall (Y-axis). It is a tiered, asymmetrical structure. The ground floor utilizes the entire 11x5 footprint, but as we move upward, the structure steps back into a smaller, offset second tier. This creates a terraced look typical of adobe architecture.

Material Strategy:
I will use Sand for the outer perimeter of the foundation to seamlessly blend the house into the surrounding desert terrain. 
I will use Cobblestone for the interior foundation to provide a sturdy, textured floor that contrasts with the soft sand outside.
I will use Stone as the primary building material for all walls and ceilings. In this desert context, Stone represents thick, sun-baked adobe or smooth sandstone, providing excellent insulation.
I will use a Chest and Bookshelves to give the interior functional, lived-in details.
I will use Stone Slabs at the very peak to break up the flat roofline and add a subtle architectural cap.

Construction Sequence:
At Y=0, I will lay down the foundation. I will create the 11x5 footprint, placing Sand around the entire outer edge to anchor the building to the dunes. Inside this ring, I will fill a 9x3 area with Cobblestone for the floor. I will intentionally place a single Sand block slightly inside the front edge to create a natural, weathered threshold for the entryway.

At Y=1, I will begin the first-floor walls using Stone. Because desert homes require thick thermal mass to keep out the midday heat, I will make this lower layer mostly solid. However, on the right side of the interior, I will carve out a small alcove and place a Chest here for secure, ground-level storage.

At Y=2 and Y=3, I will build up the main living space. I will hollow out the interior to create room to breathe, while maintaining thick Stone outer walls. At Y=2, I will construct an interior Stone pillar or partial dividing wall near the center to separate the space into two distinct areas. By Y=3, I will open up the interior space slightly more, preparing to support the ceiling.

At Y=4, I will cap the first floor with a solid 11x5 rectangle of Stone. This layer serves a dual purpose: it is the protective ceiling for the lower level and the sturdy outdoor terrace/floor for the second tier.

At Y=5, I will begin the second tier. To achieve that iconic stepped pueblo look, I will not use the full footprint. Instead, I will build a smaller 7x3 structure offset to the right side of the roof. I will place a Bookshelf here to begin furnishing this upper lookout or study room.

At Y=6 and Y=7, I will raise the walls of the second tier. I will step the walls inward slightly to give the structure a tapered, organic shape. I will stack additional Bookshelves directly on top of the one from Y=5 to create a tall bookcase, leaving a small hollow space for the occupant to stand.

At Y=8, I will construct the roof of the second tier using a solid layer of Stone, completely sealing the upper room from the harsh desert sun.

At Y=9, I will finish the build by placing two Stone Slabs on the very top of the roof. I will position these slightly off-center. This adds a minor elevation change, acting as a small parapet or sunshade detail that gives the building a finished, realistic architectural profile.

Build the Deadpool.

Footprint Analysis:
I will begin by analyzing the spatial boundaries of this structure. The X coordinates range from a minimum of 0 to a maximum of 22, giving me a total width of 23 blocks. The Y coordinates start at the ground (Y=0) and rise to Y=47, resulting in a towering height of 48 blocks. Most importantly, I must note that the Z coordinate is strictly 0 across every single instruction. Therefore, I am not building a 3D volume; I am constructing a completely flat, 2D pixel-art silhouette of the character 'Deadpool'. The structure is mostly solid, but utilizes strategic gaps (negative space) to define anatomical features and weapons.

Material Strategy:
I will use exactly one block for this entire build: minecraft:white_wool. I choose white wool because its matte, textureless appearance is perfect for 2D pixel art. It prevents the game's lighting engine from creating unwanted shadows or highlights, ensuring that Deadpool's silhouette remains crisp, stark, and easily readable against the background. 

Construction Sequence & Logic:
I will construct this silhouette layer by layer, moving from the ground up to form the character's iconic pose.

Y=0 to Y=12 (The Stance and Legs): 
I will start by building two distinct pillars to represent Deadpool's legs in a wide, dynamic combat stance. The left leg will occupy the lower X values (X=2 to X=7), and the right leg will occupy the higher X values (X=14 to X=20). As I build upward, I will slightly shift the coordinates to angle the legs. At Y=8, I will add a sudden protrusion on the far right (X=20 to X=22); I will use this to represent a weapon holster or a drawn pistol in his right hand.

Y=13 to Y=18 (The Belt and Lower Torso): 
At Y=13, I will bridge the gap between the two legs, merging them into a single solid line from X=3 to X=22. This represents his waist and utility belt. As I continue up to Y=18, I will expand the width to its absolute maximum (X=0 to X=22). I am doing this to establish the broad, muscular base of his torso and hips.

Y=19 to Y=24 (The Chest and Arms): 
Here, I must introduce negative space to give the silhouette readability. I will split the layers, leaving an empty gap around X=6 and X=7. By doing this, I will separate his left arm (X=0 to X=5) from his main chest cavity (X=8 to X=22). The right side remains thick and solid, depicting his torso turned slightly and his right arm tucked close to his body.

Y=25 to Y=31 (The Shoulders and Neck): 
At Y=25, I will close the gap, merging the left arm back into the main body. As I build up to Y=31, I will aggressively taper the outer edges inward. I will shrink the width from X=1 through X=19 down to X=4 through X=16. I am doing this to slope his shoulders and form his neck, preparing the foundation for his head.

Y=32 to Y=47 (The Masked Head and Katanas): 
Starting at Y=32, I will begin shaping the head. Between Y=34 and Y=36, I will create another deliberate gap on the far left (around X=5). I will use this isolated cluster of blocks to represent the hilts of his signature twin katanas jutting over his left shoulder. From Y=37 upward, the left side disappears entirely, and I will focus my blocks on the right side (X=5 to X=20) to form the rounded dome of his masked head and the extending katana blades. Finally, from Y=43 to Y=47, I will taper the blocks inward to X=9 through X=15, perfectly rounding off the top of his skull and the tips of his swords to complete the piece.

Build the Village House (medium).

Welcome, student. Today we are going to construct the "Village House (medium)". Before we place a single block, we must build the structure in our minds. I will walk you through my exact thought process so you can visualize how the raw coordinates translate into a sturdy, functional home.

1. Footprint Analysis
I am working within a bounding box that is 19 blocks wide (X-axis), 29 blocks deep (Z-axis), and 14 blocks tall (Y-axis). 
This is not a simple square box. I am building an L-shaped structure. It consists of a main rectangular wing and a smaller intersecting wing that juts out to the side. The interior of the house will be hollow to provide living space, while the top will feature a solid, tiered pitched roof. 

2. Material Strategy
Every block must have a logical purpose:
- Grass (A) and Dirt (B): I will use these at the very bottom to anchor the house naturally into the terrain.
- Stone (C): This is my heavy, durable material. I will use it for the foundation, the first-floor walls, and the protective roof. 
- Oak Logs (E): This is my structural skeleton. I will place logs at the corners of the walls and as horizontal beams to visually support the weight of the house.
- Oak Planks (G): This is my lightweight building material. I will use planks for the second-story walls and the interior flooring.
- Oak Leaves (D): I will scatter these outside the foundation to act as decorative bushes.
- Torches (F): I will place these inside and outside to provide light and prevent monsters from spawning.
Notice that there is no glass in our palette. Instead of glass windows, I will use strategic air gaps and stone accents to allow light and air into the home.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
Let us build it layer by layer.

Layer Y=0 (The Earth): 
I am laying down a solid foundation of Grass and Dirt. This acts as the natural ground, filling in any dips in the terrain so our house sits on a level surface.

Layers Y=1 to Y=3 (First Floor Walls): 
I will now outline the L-shaped footprint of the house. I use Stone for the primary walls to protect the ground floor from the elements. At every corner of the L-shape, I place vertical Oak Logs. This is crucial: the logs act as load-bearing pillars, giving the building structural realism. Inside, I leave the space hollow (Air) for the villager to live. At Y=3, I attach Torches to the walls for illumination and plant Oak Leaves around the exterior base to blend the heavy stone into the natural environment.

Layer Y=4 (The Floor/Ceiling Transition): 
I am now capping the first floor. I lay down a flat plane of Oak Planks to serve as the ceiling for the first floor and the floor for the second story. I border these planks with horizontal Oak Log beams. I extend these beams slightly past the stone walls to create a small overhang, which adds architectural depth and protects the lower walls from rain.

Layers Y=5 to Y=7 (Second Floor Walls): 
I am raising the second story. To prevent the house from looking too top-heavy, I switch my wall material from heavy Stone to lighter Oak Planks. I continue running my Oak Logs vertically up the corners to maintain the structural frame. At Y=6, I mix a few Stone blocks into the plank walls—these act as sturdy window frames or structural ties. I also place interior Torches here to light the upper bedroom.

Layers Y=8 to Y=13 (The Tiered Roof): 
It is time to protect the house from the weather. Starting at Y=8, I outline the top of the wooden walls with a ring of Stone and horizontal Oak Logs. 
For each subsequent layer (Y=9, Y=10, Y=11, Y=12), I step the Stone and Logs inward by one block. Because the house is L-shaped, stepping the blocks inward creates two intersecting A-frame pitched roofs. The logs act as the wooden trusses, while the stone acts as the heavy roofing material. 
Finally, at Y=13, the steps meet in the center. I place a single, solid line of Stone to form the ridge cap of the roof, sealing the structure completely.

By understanding this sequence, you can see that we are not just placing blocks at random coordinates. We are pouring a foundation, framing a skeleton, raising the walls, and capping it with a weather-proof roof. Keep this logic in your mind, and the math will naturally follow.

- White Wool (C) and Quartz Block (E): I will use these to establish the crisp, white livery of a police cruiser. Quartz provides a hard, armored look, while wool offers matte paneling for contrast.
- White Stained Glass (D): I will use this primarily for the cockpit canopy to maintain the sleek color scheme while allowing visibility. I will also use it in the lower layers to represent glowing hover-emitters, headlights, or siren bars.

Construction Sequence:

Layer Y=1: I will expand the landing gear into a narrow undercarriage using stone and stone slabs. I will keep this layer centralized and thin to maintain the floating effect, forming the lowest mechanical belly of the chassis.

Layer Y=2: I will construct the main structural floor of the space car. I will lay down a massive, mostly solid stone footprint that stretches from the front nose to the rear engine block. I will place stone slabs along the outer edges to curve the underbelly upward, giving the vehicle a sleek, aerodynamic profile.

Layer Y=3: I will introduce the police livery. I will use white wool and quartz blocks to build the lower body panels, giving the car its distinct white armor. I will place white stained glass near the front and along the sides to act as headlights and lower observation windows. The vehicle reaches its maximum width of 11 blocks in this layer to house the side-mounted hover thrusters.

Layer Y=4: I will build the beltline of the car. I will use stone to form the dashboard, side paneling, and the lower housings for the rear engines. I will leave the center area hollow to create the interior cabin space, and I will begin shaping the rear thruster exhausts at the back of the grid.

Layer Y=5: I will construct the lower half of the cockpit canopy. I will place parallel lines of white stained glass to form the side windows. At the very rear of the vehicle, I will build a wide, 9-block stone bar. This heavy structure serves as the foundational strut for a massive futuristic rear spoiler.

Layer Y=6: I will cap the cockpit cabin. I will use a combination of glass and stone slabs to create a sloped, aerodynamic roof over the driver's seat. In the rear, I will construct the intricate middle section of the spoiler, using a mix of glass, wool, and slabs to represent integrated light bars and aerodynamic fins.

Layer Y=7: I will add the final structural details. I will place a thin line of stone down the center of the canopy roof to act as a communication antenna or a mount for the police sirens. I will finish the rear by placing solid stone blocks to cap off the heavy, aggressive rear spoiler, completing the vehicle's aerodynamic profile.

Layer Y=8: I will leave this layer entirely empty, marking the upper boundary of the build and ensuring the roofline remains clean.
